name: Bernard Fitzgerald
presenting_complaint: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back

medical_history.social: Ex-smoker, quit 5 years ago. Retired carpenter.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with sudden-onset severe tearing/ripping chest pain radiating through to the interscapular back. He is pale and distressed. Blood pressure is 182/104 in the right arm but markedly lower in the left arm (a 25 mmHg differential). This is a suspected acute aortic dissection.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Pain character: sudden, maximal at onset, tearing/ripping, radiating to the back — classic for dissection
Associated features: syncope, limb weakness/paraesthesia, abdominal pain (branch-vessel involvement)
Risk factors: hypertension, connective tissue disease/family history of sudden death, previous aortic disease
Explicitly state that usual ACS treatment (antiplatelets/anticoagulation) would harm this patient
Key negatives: no obvious ischaemic ECG evolution, screen for neurological deficit
objective: BP measured in BOTH arms — document the inter-arm differential
Assess pulses in all four limbs; check for pulse deficit
Cardiovascular exam: new diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, signs of tamponade (muffled sounds, raised JVP, hypotension)
Neurological exam for focal deficit (carotid/spinal artery involvement)
12-lead ECG (may mimic inferior infarct) and portable CXR (widened mediastinum)
assessment: Acute aortic dissection — high clinical probability given tearing pain, inter-arm BP differential
Differentiate from STEMI/ACS — critical because treatment differs completely
Consider complications: aortic regurgitation, cardiac tamponade, malperfusion, rupture
plan: Two large-bore IV cannulas, group and crossmatch, cardiac monitor, opioid analgesia (e.g. morphine IV titrated) — FIRST actions
CT aortogram is the definitive investigation — arrange urgently

BP and heart-rate control on senior instruction: rate-control FIRST (IV beta-blocker e.g. esmolol/metoprolol) to HR under 60, THEN reduce systolic to 100-120 mmHg (e.g. GTN/sodium nitroprusside infusion)
ECG and CXR (widened mediastinum) while arranging CT
Escalate immediately: call ED consultant, cardiothoracic surgery and ICU
Strict BP monitoring, analgesia, and prepare for potential theatre/transfer

critical_errors: Giving aspirin, other antiplatelets or anticoagulants before aortic dissection has been excluded — can cause fatal haemorrhage/extension
Dropping blood pressure with a vasodilator BEFORE beta-blockade (unopposed reflex tachycardia increases aortic wall stress)
Treating the presentation as a simple STEMI and giving thrombolysis
must_not_miss: Aortic dissection identified and CT aortogram arranged
